title: Va'etchanan: the Shema whole (Deuteronomy 6:4–9)
hook: love God with all your heart, soul and might
tomorrow: Va'etchanan: at home and on the way (Deuteronomy 6:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' warning: guard what you saw and tell it. Your line was don't forget what you saw. Did you write a memory down? Today, the words Jews say every morning and every night, in their home chapter. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

Many Jewish children learn the Shema before they can read. Six Hebrew words, said with a hand over the eyes. It's said at bedtime, said in the morning service and the evening service, and for many centuries it has been the words Jews hoped to say at the very end of life. The first line is often said on its own, like a motto. In the Torah it isn't on its own at all. It sits in the middle of Moses' farewell, in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy, and the very next word opens a paragraph. Today, the line and the word that follows it.
screen: `SIX WORDS, A HAND OVER THE EYES.` → `MORNING, NIGHT, AND THE END.` → `THE WORD THAT FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: First the line, in the old Jewish translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Then, without a pause in the text: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The first Hebrew word of that second verse is today's word. V'ahavta. And thou shalt love. It names the whole paragraph that Jews say right after the Shema. And it raises a question the rabbis took seriously: can love be commanded? The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, answers by taking the three phrases one at a time. With all thy heart: the Hebrew spells heart here with a doubled letter, levavcha, and the Mishnah hears two hearts, so love God with both your inclinations, the good one and the selfish one. Your whole messy self, not just your best moods. With all thy soul: even if your life is taken. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying under Roman torture, said the Shema and drew out the final word, one, until his breath ended. With all thy might: the Mishnah reads it as with all your money, your resources. And it adds one more: for whatever measure is measured out to you, good or bad, give thanks. So the command isn't to feel warm. It's to bring everything, the good impulses and the bad, your life, your wallet, your luck, into one direction. The paragraph that follows tells how: these words on your heart, taught to your children, on your doorposts. That's tomorrow.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `V'AHAVTA: AND THOU SHALT LOVE.` · `BOTH HEARTS, YOUR LIFE, YOUR MIGHT.` · `EVERY MEASURE, GOOD OR BAD.` · then, large: `WITH ALL YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the Shema and V'ahavta, slowly. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can cover your eyes and say the first line, Shema Yisrael, in Hebrew or English, then the next verse, word by word, with a breath between each phrase. If you don't pray, listen to the three phrases as questions instead. What would all your heart include, even the parts you're not proud of? What do you give your life to? Where does your might, your money and your time, actually go? The bell holds the time.
V'ahavta. And thou shalt love. The verse after the Shema, and the name of the paragraph said with it, morning and night.
Your line: with all your heart. Today, bring one thing you usually hold back, a mood, an hour, a little money, into what you love. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews recite the Shema and the V'ahavta paragraph in the morning and evening services and at bedtime, many covering their eyes for the first line; the passage is also written inside the mezuzah and tefillin.

myth: the Shema is a standalone line with nothing after it
it's Deuteronomy 6:4, and v'ahavta follows straight on in 6:5.
the Mishnah reads with all thy might as with all your money
the Mishnah says to give thanks only for the good
for whatever measure is measured out to you, good or bad.

fork.setup: the verse commands love with all thy heart. the Hebrew spells heart with a doubled letter. what does the Mishnah make of it?
options: love God only with your best self.
love God with both inclinations, the good and the selfish.
fork.reveal: levavcha, two hearts: love God with the good inclination and the selfish one too.

original.note: Hebrew: and thou shalt love. the first word of Deuteronomy 6:5, naming the paragraph after the Shema.

trapdoor: what you thought: love God means feel warmly toward God.
what it means: bring everything into one direction: both your inclinations, your life, your money, your luck.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 9:5 reads levavcha's doubled bet as two inclinations and me'odecha as money.

sources.quoted: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.
And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

notes: Deuteronomy 6:4–5 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Mishnah Berakhot 9:5: two inclinations (from the doubled bet in levavcha), 'even if He takes your soul', 'with all your money', and 'for every measure He measures out to you, thank Him'; paraphrased.
Rabbi Akiva's death with the Shema: Berakhot 61b; confirm phrasing that he prolonged the word echad.
The claim that the Shema is said with the hand over the eyes and at bedtime is common practice; customs vary.
Hook's 'six Hebrew words' counts Shema Yisrael Adonai Eloheinu Adonai Echad.
Audit (second sample): replaced the unsourced claim 'most people know the first line; fewer know it isn't a standalone slogan' with a plain description.
